catalog_quote: 2. Tone and Stress 2a. Tone Tone is both lexical and grammatical. In ZANDE two main tone levels have been established ... 2b. Stress In ZANDE stress usually falls on the first syllable of disyllabic or trisyllabic words, combined in some dialects (and in BARAMBU) with slight lengthening. In some words in BARAMBU, however, it falls on the final syllable; see baa above. Stress never falls on Prefixes. 3. Word Shape Most words in their simplest form are disyllabic: CVCV ... [CVV words] frequent (more frequent in BARAMBU and PAMBIA than in ZANDE); here any vowel may be final. ... [sec. 4b Nouns:] ... together in some ZANDE dialects; Tone Classes have also been noted in BARAMBU-PAMBIA. [sec. 1 (vowels), pp. 141-142, the passage that 'see baa above' points to:] Diphthongs and long vowels occur in final position in many words, e.g.: ZANDE báa father, ... bowels, mál rain, ŋgúa tree; cf. bá pla…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Barambu is a tone language (lexical and grammatical tone); a non-contrastive word stress usually falls on the first syllable of di- and trisyllabic words and is realised in Barambu with slight vowel lengthening; a minority of Barambu words carry it on the final syllable instead; prefixes are never stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: 'In some words in BARAMBU, however, it falls on the final syllable; see baa above' (the word baa is discussed earlier in the chapter, in the vowel/length section, not recovered). 'Stress never falls on Prefixes.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: disyllabic and trisyllabic words; stress accompanied in Barambu by slight lengthening; prefixes never stressed. Statement is made for the Zande group as a whole with Barambu singled out; Tucker & Bryan's data on Barambu were, by their own 1956 admission, 'still fragmentary'. Language is tonal (2a: tone lexical and grammatical; tone classes noted in Barambu-Pambia), so 'stress' here is a non-contrastive prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is in Tucker & Bryan's Zande Group chapter and names BARAMBU (= Barambu proper, bara1361) explicitly; Tucker & Bryan elsewhere lump 'BARAMBU-PAMBIA' (Pambia = pamb1243), but the stress sentence names Barambu alone and Pambia is not mentioned in it. Tucker & Hackett 1959 index abbreviations keep Barambu (B.) and Pambia (P.) separate, with the stress page (179) under B. only. Older sources call the language Abarambo / A-Barambo (Junker 1889, Brugger 1912, Czekanowski 1924).
